questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer:
Three motivations:
1: Exploring new cultures
2: Personal learning
3: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Canada was a country I've found particularly compelling since I was a teenager, and eventually, that interest narrowed down some more into Toronto, specifically -- I read that the University of Toronto, specifically, was an exceptional university, so I couldn't help but narrow my focus a little more, and so that's where I chose to study.
Another crucial aspect was the immense interest in the country itself, particularly the province of Ontario, and I wanted to study in a very central and urban place in order to get the most in-your-face cultural experience that I could. Furthermore, I also very much wanted to better understand what it would be like to be a long-term resident in Ontario, as I plan to move there at some point in my early 30s.
Lastly, I was searching for a place where I might experience some more unconventional ways of learning and of being instructed, and I figured there was a higher likelihood that I might find those unconventional methods at a university in North America--and at the University of Toronto, I certainly did, and it truly was a blast!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, this my time as an exchange student at the U of T has influenced me for the better, and by "for the better", I mean to an extent that I expect will affect my future in a very, very beautiful way.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. I had no pressing questions or uncertainties upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a virtual "Inbound Exchange Orientation". The information I was given at this orientation was very helpful and even relieving throughout the term over there.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It wasn't that hard--I found an affordable Airbnb, and it was barely a half-hour walk from campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's not as convenient as living on-campus (though if your off-campus home is not too far away, it's not that big a deal). Furthermore, when living off-campus, you will probably have much fewer spontaneous interactions with fellow students, which can be a bit discouraging. However, there are some advantages to living off-campus. For example, it depends on where you're going, but I found that living off-campus can be a whole lot cheaper if you find the right place. Also, if there are certain places/things you're especially interested in, you can stay at an off-campus residency closer to those places/things, which can be fun when it comes to exploring the place around the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: On-campus student housing was available with no problems, except that it was very expensive, hence my choosing to live at an Airbnb as an alternative.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was fairly straightforward. At the U of T, what I had to do was send in individual applications for each of the four courses I wanted to take. Then, if you later wanted to switch one course with another, you had to send a course application form AND a course drop form--this was something I had to do, which was fine, really. I got a bit nervous later on because I was on the waiting list for half of the courses I had applied for, but I was high up on those lists and eventually, I got into every course I wanted to get into.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: When it came to course registration, there was a sort of PowerPoint / PDF with a step-by-step process, which was fairly helpful. There was likely other forms of assistance readily available, though I didn't really end up needing them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I knew what to do, and I did those things, and I got what I wanted, so I was quite successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
My main advice would be this:
Talk to the right people, pay close attention to advice and instructions--basically, just make sure to know about *everything* you need to do, how to register for the courses you truly feel that you want that are available to you, and to be aware of any and all deadlines. Otherwise, it can be very, very stressful, and something you weren't otherwise expecting could pop up seemingly out of nowhere, making for a much more awkward process. And, of course, I would suggest to take courses you think you would enjoy a lot, because traveling and living in a social environment that's very different from the one you're used to can already be quite exhausting at times, but that's just me I guess.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: While the workload was very difficult to bear, I found it almost life-changing, really. The professors I had over there were wonderful, and, alongside the more purely academic approaches, I got to experience a very free/creative form of learning and applying knowledge in academic projects. The overall experience was exceptionally eye-opening, and I will be carrying it around everywhere I go.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The four courses were on varying 300-levels:
Medieval Literature - 311
Contemporary Poetry - 349
Contemporary American Fiction - 365
Environmental Imagination - 377

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching at the University of Toronto was, from my experience, much more free in the sense that there was a lot of space for creative approaches to complex problems and academic projects. I felt like I was given more chances to apply aspects of my own individual personality (not just my intellectual abilities) to projects I was tasked with.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Medieval Literature (ENG311 H1 S)
Contemporary Poetry (ENG349 H1 S)
Contemporary American Fiction (ENG365 H1 S)
The Environmental Imagination (ENG377 H1 S)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Well, I can really only speak for the courses that I was enrolled in during this semester.  And, really, I recommend all of four of them. However, I didn't enjoy Contemporary Poetry as much as the others, but that's mainly because I don't like poetry -- though, with that said, if an exchange student is especially interested in improving their close-reading skills significantly, I would very highly recommend taking Contemporary Poetry, as it often deals with some very cryptic texts with extremely compressed meaning.
Out of all four of them, Contemporary American Fiction is the one I would recommend the very most! We had to go through soooo much material, but it was so wild and fascinating, and the professor that in that course was a total blast, and he was exceptionally encouraging. Contemporary American Fiction was most certainly my favorite course at the U of T during my semester there.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went to get a quick check-up at the dentist for some gum/tooth aches I was experiencing pretty much non-stop -- since the health insurance plan doesn't cover dental, I had to pay about 800kr for that check-up ... and it wasn't even a full check-up, just one that was concentrated on area in pain.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I honestly didn't expect that cheese would be so expensive in Toronto. On the other hand, juice was almost weirdly cheap. Chips were also slightly cheaper, though I was sort of expecting that for some reason.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The extracurricular clubs I wanted to get involved with were closed down due to the Covid-19 pandemic, which was a major bummer. But, since I know they probably would've been pretty awesome if they were available to me, I give this a neutral "3" (if the clubs were available, I would have rated "5", I'm almost certain of that--the amount of clubs available at the U of T is seriously nuts--there's even a trading-card-playing club where people play Yu-Gi-Oh, Magic: The Gathering, etc.)

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There would have been far more of such activities available if it weren't for the pandemic. However, the city of Toronto itself is extremely culturally diverse, so cultural activities at the U of T are probably rich and plentiful. As far as athletic and social activities go, I'm not even a hundred percent sure. The classes and their projects can be very social. I do believe I saw a group of students carrying out some lacrosse practice.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Example: I can recommend checking out novelty restaurants, such as "Stormcrow Manor", which is like a big geeky restaurant, and they make pretty awesome science fiction and fantasy themed food. Basically, there are several "weird" restaurants worth checking out in Toronto.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would certainly recommend the Royal Ontario Museum, the Art Gallery of Ontario, and Ripley's Aquarium.
There are also many interesting restaurants to visit, such as Stormcrow Manor (a geeky restaurant with themed meals and drinks--they make an amazing French onion soup, too).
There are also a lot of interesting stores, such as The Monkey's Paw, a rare book store known for having some pretty weird and weirdly specific books (went there several times).
The parks in Toronto are also just amazing--I went to High Park to go birdwatching, and there is so much beautiful life in that city, it's truly astounding.
Also, just walking around the city of Toronto with no particular goal in mind can be very interesting, as there really is a lot to do, and it can be fun to just "figure it out" as you go along, and perhaps find something that really resonates with you.
It's all pretty cool.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It wasn't easy, but it wasn't excruciatingly hard either. Of course, my mother tongue is English, which is what most people speak in Toronto, so that certainly made it easier for me to adapt.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: All I would say is to socialize with other students in whatever way you're comfortable with (though it always helps to be aware of certain social formalities if there are any that are especially different from the ones you're used to--just to make you feel like you're on more solid ground).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Some formalities were a bit surprising. For example, total strangers would say "how are you?" as part of a greeting--for example, "Hi there, how are you?" "Hi, I'm good, how are you?" "I'm good, thanks" ... it was a bit awkward to get used to, and I don't think I stayed long enough for it to completely stop feeling weird to me. However, I adapted, and it was fine, though very occasionally I got a bit of a stare for not reciprocating the "how are you?" bit. Tipping culture was also a bit challenging, as I'm really just not used to that, and sometimes if I felt I didn't tip "enough", I would feel a bit guilty. I would certainly recommend looking up Canadian tipping conventions.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Something I noticed was that a lot of people in Toronto were very, very good with small-talk, and because of that, social environments can be quite inviting, which I very much enjoyed, particularly since I'm not always very keen on initiating conversations. I can often be quite nervous and awkward around strangers, but in Toronto, that wasn't too much of a burden because it was just surprisingly easier to communicate with people (as long as they were friendly). Of course, you can never generalize, but this is what I experienced when it came to interacting with strangers. It was very nice, and it was interesting.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: If you're not already well used to a consistently heavy workload (and by heavy, I mean *heavy*), be prepared, and make sure to organize leisure-time and study-time in a way that reduces stress without sacrificing efficiency/productivity while you study at the U of T.
2: Don't forget to have a good time--I'm aware this may be a given, but there are so many fun, interesting things to do and experience in Toronto (and at the university as well), and between the periods of hours-long work, you're definitely going to want to find good ways to unwind.
3: The campus I was attending is totally beautiful and full of smart, interesting students--so, I would highly recommend interacting with fellow students and being proactive during group projects, as there's so very much that can be learned even from the other students there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Besides what I've said in preceding comments, not that I can think of at this exact moment.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Paying attention during class, studying sufficiently--making it through the heavy, heavy workload was extremely rewarding, as I had no idea I was capable of doing that as successfully as I did. That was probably the most rewarding part of it all, and it has certainly improved my work ethic considerably. It's tough as hell, but in the end, having really applied myself, I feel quite proud. I feel like I'm capable of more than I was before. I'm very happy about this.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Again, the workload. Since several exams are dispersed throughout the semester, I had to almost constantly study one or several exams all while getting through near unending heaps of homework.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Not that I can think of.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
